entity.name: Soham Mitra
entity.description: Independent developer in Mumbai, India, building Vlocalhost AI: a meeting recorder that records, transcribes and summarises entirely on the user's own machine. No audio, transcript or note is uploaded anywhere, there is no account and no backend, and the core is AGPL-3.0 with the source public so the part that touches your audio can be read and verified. Built for people who cannot send a meeting to a cloud at all.

projects.name: Vlocalhost Core
projects.description: An on-device meeting notetaker for Windows and macOS. Audio is captured locally, transcribed with faster-whisper on the endpoint, and summarised by a local model the user chooses; the transcript is written to disk before the summary is attempted, so a missing model never costs you the meeting. Notes are Markdown and plain text in a folder you pick, not rows in a database. There is no telemetry, no crash reporting and no analytics, because there is no endpoint to send them to. The app is also an MCP server, so an assistant such as Claude or Cursor can start a recording, follow the live transcript and search your own notes without any of it leaving the machine. Every release publishes a SHA-256 for each file and a GitHub build attestation, so the bytes you downloaded can be checked against the bytes that were built.

channels.description: Grants and sponsorship are arranged directly by email at voiceit@vlocal.host. No public payment endpoint is published yet; one will be added here when it exists rather than listed speculatively.

plans.name: Code signing and notarization (floor: 1 of 2)
plans.description:
The most-reported problem with the project, and the one thing money fixes outright. Windows builds are unsigned and macOS builds are ad-hoc signed and not notarized, so both operating systems warn the user that the app cannot be verified. For a tool whose entire proposition is that it can be trusted with confidential meetings, that first-run warning does real damage. This covers an Apple Developer Program membership, a Windows code-signing certificate with the hardware token its issuance now requires, and the signing pipeline work. Until it is funded the project publishes a SHA-256 per file and a GitHub build attestation instead, and says so up front rather than letting people discover it. This is USD 1,200 of the USD 3,700 minimum ask, alongside the Indian-language benchmark plan.

The ask in this manifest is a range, not a single figure. The floor is USD 3,700 -- the two small one-time plans together -- which is the least that produces a result someone can point at. The ceiling is USD 100,000, the full scaling and testing programme. Every line is independent and any subset can be funded on its own.

plans.name: Indian-language transcription benchmark (floor: 2 of 2)
plans.description:
The project is built in India and cannot currently claim Indian-language support, because Whisper is weak on Indic speech and on code-mixing and nobody has measured how weak. Open-weight Indian-language models now exist that could run on the same device, and the app already supports bringing your own voice model, so this is a measurement problem rather than an architecture problem. This funds building a fixture set of real multi-speaker meeting audio across Indian languages, running the existing benchmark harness across candidate models, and publishing the word-error-rate results in full including the ones that do not flatter the project. This is the smallest useful version of the work, offered for the case where only a small amount is available. It is contained within the scaling and testing plan in this manifest and should not be added to it. This is USD 2,500 of the USD 3,700 minimum ask, alongside the code-signing plan.

The ask in this manifest is a range, not a single figure. The floor is USD 3,700 -- the two small one-time plans together -- which is the least that produces a result someone can point at. The ceiling is USD 100,000, the full scaling and testing programme. Every line is independent and any subset can be funded on its own.

plans.name: Scaling and testing -- the full programme (ceiling)
plans.description:
The full programme, itemised, because a round number with a vague label is not something a reviewer can check. The largest line is engineering time, deliberately: the hardware and services below are useless without someone paid to use them, and a grant that funds only equipment for a bootstrapped project quietly assumes free labour.

Engineering time (~USD 44,000). Roughly a year of focused full-time work at Indian rates, on the four things a teardown against three competing products showed matter most: rewriting audio capture onto the native device format, on-device speaker diarization, encryption of transcripts at rest, and integrating open-weight Indian-language models. These are known, scoped pieces of work, not exploration.

Device lab and audio-hardware matrix (~USD 18,000). Almost every serious defect in a desktop recorder is hardware-specific and cannot be found without the hardware. That comparison found our microphone path runs through a legacy host API at roughly 120 ms where a well-funded rival opens WASAPI at the device's native rate in about 3 ms, that we do no echo cancellation, and that a headset plugged in mid-meeting is untested. Reproducing that needs Apple silicon and Intel Macs, Windows laptops old and new, USB audio interfaces, Bluetooth headsets and docking stations.

Indian-language corpus and evaluation (~USD 18,000). Recording and licensing real multi-speaker meeting audio across Indian languages, with consent and fair payment to the speakers, plus the compute to score candidate on-device models against it. Read speech is not meeting speech, and public corpora do not cover code-mixing the way an actual standup does. This line includes and supersedes the smaller Indic benchmark plan in this manifest; the two are alternatives, not additive.

Independent security review (~USD 8,000). An external audit of the central claim, that no audio, transcript or note is transmitted anywhere, published in full including anything it finds. The claim is worth exactly as much as somebody else's willingness to test it.

Cross-platform CI and release automation (~USD 7,000). Hosted macOS runners, reproducible signed builds and an automated test matrix, so a release is verified before it ships rather than after a user reports it.

Accessibility and localisation (~USD 5,000). Screen-reader support and interface translation, which matter more than usual for a tool whose users include people who cannot use a cloud transcript at all.

Partial funding is genuinely useful and the lines are independent: any subset can be funded on its own, and the smaller plans in this manifest exist for exactly that case.

The ask in this manifest is a range, not a single figure. The floor is USD 3,700 -- the two small one-time plans together -- which is the least that produces a result someone can point at. The ceiling is USD 100,000, the full scaling and testing programme. Every line is independent and any subset can be funded on its own.

plans.name: Ongoing maintenance and support
plans.description: Keeping the recorder working across Windows and macOS updates, audio-device changes and model releases, answering issues, and keeping the dependency set pinned, audited and reflected in the published SBOM. Any amount.
